paragraphs: It is part of the essence of a democratic army, as I shall show later, to be very large in proportion to the population it belongs to. On the other hand, people who live in democratic times seldom choose a military life. Democratic nations are therefore soon led to abandon voluntary recruiting in favor of compulsory enlistment. Their social condition forces them to the latter, and it is easy to foresee that all of them will eventually adopt it. When military service is compulsory, the burden falls equally and without exception on the whole community. This too is a necessary result of the social condition of these nations and of their ideas. The government can do almost anything it likes, provided it addresses the whole community at once. It is the unequal distribution of the weight, not the weight itself, that usually provokes resistance. But since military service is shared by all citizens, the plain consequence is that each of them stays on active duty only a few years. So it is in the nature of things that the soldier in democracies merely passes through the army, whereas among most aristocratic nations the military is a profession that the soldier chooses, or has forced upon him, for life.

This has important consequences. Among the soldiers of a democratic army, some develop a taste for military life. But the majority were enlisted against their will and are always ready to go back home. They do not regard themselves as seriously committed to the military profession, and they are always thinking of leaving it. Such men do not take on the needs, and share only half the passions, that this way of life breeds. They adapt to their military duties, but their minds remain attached to the interests and duties that occupied them in civilian life. So they do not absorb the spirit of the army; rather, they bring the spirit of the community at large into the army and keep it there. In democratic nations the private soldiers stay most like civilians. The habits of the nation have the firmest hold on them, and public opinion has the most influence. It is chiefly through the private soldiers that a democratic army may be filled with the love of freedom and respect for rights, once these principles have been successfully instilled in the people at large. The opposite happens among aristocratic nations, where the soldiery eventually have nothing in common with their fellow citizens and live among them as strangers, often as enemies. In aristocratic armies the officers are the conservative element, because the officers alone have kept a close tie with civil society and never give up their intention of returning to it sooner or later. In democratic armies the private soldiers are in that position, for the same reason.

In these same democratic armies, by contrast, it often happens that the officers acquire tastes and needs wholly different from those of the nation. The explanation is this. Among democratic nations, the man who becomes an officer cuts every tie that bound him to civilian life. He leaves it for good and has no interest in returning. His true country is the army, since he owes everything he has to the rank he has reached in it. So he follows the army’s fortunes, rises or falls with it, and from then on directs all his hopes to that quarter alone. Because an officer’s needs differ from the country’s, he may passionately desire war, or work to bring about a revolution, at the very moment when the nation most wants stability and peace. There are nevertheless some causes that soothe this restless and warlike spirit. Ambition is universal and continual among democratic nations, but we have seen that it is seldom great. A man born into the lower classes of the community who has risen from the ranks to become an officer has already taken an enormous step. He has gained a foothold in a sphere above the one he occupied in civilian life, and he has acquired rights that most democratic nations will always regard as inalienable. *a He is willing to pause after such a great effort and enjoy what he has won. The fear of risking what he already has dampens his desire to gain what he does not yet have. Having overcome the first and greatest obstacle to his advancement, he accepts the slowness of his progress with less impatience. His ambition will cool more and more as the growing distinction of his rank teaches him that he has more to put at risk. If I am not mistaken, the least warlike part of a democratic army, and also the least revolutionary, will always be its senior commanders. [Footnote a: The position of officers is in fact much more secure among democratic nations than elsewhere. The lower a man’s personal standing, the greater the relative importance of his military grade, and the more just and necessary it is that the laws secure his enjoyment of that rank.]

But what I have just said about officers and soldiers does not apply to a numerous class that, in every army, fills the space between them. I mean the non-commissioned officers. This class, which played no part in history until the present century, is destined from now on, I think, to play a fairly important one. Like the officers, non-commissioned officers have broken, in their minds, every tie that bound them to civilian life. Like them, they give themselves to the service permanently, and perhaps make it even more exclusively the object of all their desires. But non-commissioned officers have not yet reached a firm and lofty post where they can pause and breathe more freely before going on to further promotion. By the very nature of his duties, which never change, a non-commissioned officer is condemned to an obscure, cramped, comfortless and precarious existence. So far he sees nothing of military life but its dangers. He knows nothing of it but its privations and its discipline, which are harder to bear than dangers. He suffers more from his present miseries because he knows that the structure of society and of the army allows him to rise above them. He may in fact obtain his commission at any time and step at once into command, honors, independence, rights and enjoyments. Not only does this object of his hopes seem immensely important to him, but he is never sure of reaching it until it is actually his. The grade he holds is by no means permanent. He is always entirely at the arbitrary pleasure of his commanding officer, since the needs of discipline imperiously require this. A slight fault or a whim can strip him in an instant of the fruits of many years of toil and effort. Until he reaches the grade he aspires to, he has accomplished nothing; only when he reaches it does his career seem to begin. A desperate ambition cannot fail to be kindled in a man who is goaded on without pause by his youth, his wants, his passions, the spirit of his age, his hopes and his fears. Non-commissioned officers are therefore set on war, on war always and at any cost. If war is denied them, they want revolutions that suspend the authority of established regulations, so that, helped by the general confusion and the political passions of the time, they can get rid of their superior officers and take their places. Nor is it impossible for them to bring about such a crisis, because their common origin and habits give them great influence over the soldiers, however different the soldiers’ passions and desires may be.

It would be a mistake to suppose that these various characteristics of officers, non-commissioned officers and men belong to a particular time or country. They will always appear, in every period and among all democratic nations. In every democratic army the non-commissioned officers will be the worst representatives of the country’s peaceful and orderly spirit, and the private soldiers the best. The private soldiers will carry into military life the strength or weakness of the national customs and will faithfully mirror the community. If the community is ignorant and weak, they will let their leaders draw them into disorder, either unwittingly or against their will. If it is educated and energetic, the community itself will keep them within the bounds of order.
